---
title: "Quiz: denoising by wavelet shrinkage"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Hard threshold: keep $w$ if $|w| > t$, else 0. Soft threshold: $\operatorname{sign}(w)\max(|w| - t, 0)$.

---

**Q1.** Why does thresholding wavelet coefficients separate signal from noise?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How are signal and noise spread over the coefficients?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The image is sparse: its energy sits in a few large coefficients. White noise, in an orthonormal basis, puts noise of the same standard deviation $\sigma_n$ into every coefficient. So small coefficients are mostly noise and large ones mostly signal; killing the small ones removes most of the noise and little of the signal.
:::

---

**Q2.** Soft-threshold $(4, -0.5, -2.5, 1)$ with $t = 1$. Then hard-threshold it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Soft subtracts $t$ from the magnitude of the survivors.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Soft: $(3, 0, -1.5, 0)$. Hard: $(4, 0, -2.5, 0)$ ($|1| = t$ is not above $t$, so it is killed).
:::

---

**Q3.** Which threshold rule tends to leave isolated blips, and which lowers the contrast of edges? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to a noise coefficient just above $t$, and to a large signal coefficient?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Hard thresholding leaves blips: a noise coefficient just above $t$ survives at full size and shows up as a small wavelet-shaped spot. Soft thresholding shrinks every survivor by $t$, including the large coefficients at edges, so edges lose contrast; a surviving noise coefficient becomes tiny instead of a blip.
:::

---

**Q4.** What is the universal threshold for a $512 \times 512$ image with $\sigma_n = 10$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N}$ with $N = 512^2 = 2^{18}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\ln N = 18\ln 2 = 12.48$, $\sqrt{2 \cdot 12.48} = 5.00$, so $t \approx 50$ grey levels.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is $\sigma_n$ estimated with the **median** of the finest D band and not with its standard deviation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What else is in that band besides noise?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The band also contains a few large signal coefficients at edges and corners. They inflate the standard deviation a lot, but barely move the median. For pure Gaussian noise the median of $|w|$ is $0.6745\,\sigma_n$, hence the divisor.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why is the coarsest approximation (LL) not thresholded?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How large are LL coefficients compared with $\sigma_n$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
LL coefficients are averages over large blocks: large compared with $\sigma_n$, so they would survive anyway, and soft thresholding would only shift the brightness. The noise per pixel in the block average is small; the noise to remove sits in the details.
:::

---

**Q7.** What is cycle spinning, and which artefact does it reduce?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The decimated transform is shift-variant.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Shift the image, denoise, shift back, and average over many shifts. Thresholding errors of the decimated transform are tied to its grid (blocks with Haar, small ringing patterns with Daubechies); for different shifts they fall in different places and average out.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* For which energy is soft thresholding with $t = \lambda$ the exact minimiser, and why does the problem split into one scalar problem per coefficient?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Orthonormal transforms preserve distances.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\tfrac12\|y - x\|^2 + \lambda\|Wx\|_1$ with $W$ orthonormal. Since $\|y - x\| = \|Wy - Wx\|$, with $c = Wx$ and $w = Wy$ the energy is $\sum_i\big(\tfrac12(w_i - c_i)^2 + \lambda|c_i|\big)$, a sum of independent terms; each is minimised by $c_i = \operatorname{sign}(w_i)\max(|w_i| - \lambda, 0)$.
:::
